impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent holder's conditioning of patent licenses on exclusive purchase of unpatented products constitutes unlawful tying under the Sherman Act, and whether the 'nonstaple goods' defense applies when the tied products have substantial non-infringing uses.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed a jury verdict finding Ingevity liable for unlawful tying under the Sherman Act for conditioning licenses to its fuel-vapor canister patent on customers' exclusive purchase of Ingevity's unpatented carbon honeycomb products. The court upheld that the honeycomb products had substantial non-infringing uses (e.g., air-intake systems outside the patent's scope), defeating the nonstaple goods defense. This ruling reinforces that patent holders cannot leverage patents to compel purchases of unpatented goods with substantial independent commercial uses.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of anticompetitive tying by patent holders can challenge the nonstaple goods defense by demonstrating substantial non-infringing uses of the tied product, potentially recovering antitrust damages.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders who bundle patent licenses with exclusive purchasing requirements for unpatented products face significant antitrust liability if those products have uses outside the scope of the patent.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that patent claims for using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache were invalid for failure to satisfy written-description and enablement requirements under 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed JMOL of invalidity of Teva's headache patents covering methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies (the active ingredient in Teva's Ajovy) to treat headache, where a jury had found willful infringement by Lilly. The court held that the specification's disclosure of one humanized antibody, combined with known prior-art methods of humanization and known murine anti-CGRP antibodies, was sufficient under both written description and enablement. This is a major ruling in the ongoing Ajovy/CGRP migraine treatment patent dispute worth potentially billions in damages.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical patent holders benefit from a more permissive standard for written description and enablement when the specification discloses known methods and a representative embodiment, even if only one specific species is disclosed.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar manufacturers face broader patent protection for biologic drug claims that rely on known-in-the-art methods, potentially delaying market entry.

impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to detecting anomalous program executions by comparing emulated function calls to a model are abstract under Alice step one, and whether damages for foreign sales of cybersecurity software are recoverable under U.S. patent law.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million jury verdict for Columbia, holding that patents covering methods for detecting anomalous program executions (cybersecurity technology licensed to Norton/Symantec) are directed to abstract ideas at Alice step one, requiring remand for step-two analysis. The court also held that damages based on Norton's foreign sales were improperly awarded, limiting patent damages to domestic conduct. The decision significantly impacts cybersecurity and software patent enforcement and restricts extraterritorial patent damages.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies defending against software patent assertions benefit from the court's application of Alice to cybersecurity detection methods and the limitation on foreign-sales damages.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the software and cybersecurity space face heightened risk of invalidity under § 101, and universities and other patent licensors may lose significant damages when the accused infringer generates substantial foreign revenue.

impacts.caseName: GoTV Streaming, LLC v. Netflix, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to a server that tailors content presentation specifications to a wireless device's screen size and capabilities are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that GoTV's patents claiming methods and systems for tailoring streamed content to a device's capabilities are ineligible under § 101, reversing a $2.5 million jury verdict against Netflix. The court found the claims directed to the abstract idea of adapting content to device capabilities and lacking an inventive concept. This ruling required reversal of the entire judgment in favor of Netflix and impacts the enforceability of adaptive streaming technology patents broadly.
impacts.positiveImplications: Streaming platforms and content delivery companies gain protection against patent assertions covering basic adaptive content delivery functionality.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the streaming technology space face significant § 101 challenges when claims cover content adaptation to device characteristics, a potentially broad category of streaming patents.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent holder's infringement claims based on the design of multicore processors are barred by extraterritoriality when the accused products are manufactured and tested abroad, and whether doctrine of equivalents was properly applied.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed-in-part the district court's grant of summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's multicore processor patent against Intel, finding genuine disputes of material fact as to the extraterritoriality defense. The court also addressed the striking of VLSI's damages expert theories. This high-profile dispute in the ongoing VLSI-Intel patent wars has significant implications for semiconductor patent enforcement where design, manufacturing, and testing occur across multiple jurisdictions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting semiconductor and processor patents benefit from a narrower application of the extraterritoriality defense when accused products are ultimately sold domestically.
impacts.negativeImplications: Chip manufacturers with global design and manufacturing operations face continued exposure to U.S. patent infringement claims even when key accused activities occur abroad.

impacts.caseName: Global Tubing LLC v. Tenaris Coiled Tubes LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether genuine disputes of material fact preclude summary judgment on inequitable conduct and Walker Process antitrust fraud claims related to the procurement of coiled tubing patents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment on both Global Tubing's inequitable conduct defense and its Walker Process antitrust fraud claim against Tenaris, finding genuine disputes of material fact on both issues. The court held that questions remained about whether Tenaris withheld material prior art (the CYMAX Documents) during patent prosecution with intent to deceive, and whether Tenaris's conduct constituted attempted monopolization. The case returns key IP-antitrust issues to trial in the oil and gas equipment sector.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies facing patent infringement claims gain leverage when prior art concealment during prosecution can give rise to both inequitable conduct defenses and Walker Process antitrust counterclaims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders who obtained patents without disclosing acquired prior art face dual exposure to inequitable conduct findings and antitrust liability for attempted monopolization.

impacts.caseName: Apple Inc. v. International Trade Commission
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple Watch models incorporating blood oxygen measurement functionality infringed Masimo's patents and properly issued a limited exclusion order barring their importation.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple Watches with blood oxygen measurement features infringed Masimo's patents covering wearable pulse oximetry devices, upholding a limited exclusion order barring importation. The court found no error in the Commission's domestic industry determination, validity rulings, or infringement findings. This decision sustains a major trade enforcement action that directly impacts Apple's ability to import and sell Apple Watch models with blood oxygen features in the United States.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with domestic industry investments gain confirmation that ITC exclusion orders remain a powerful enforcement tool against major technology importers.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major technology companies face significant commercial disruption when ITC exclusion orders block importation of flagship consumer products, requiring costly design-arounds or licensing.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action when it missed the deadline for seeking a stay of the original action involving the same parties and issues.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for obtaining a mandatory stay of a parallel district court action under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) by dismissing and refiling the district court action to restart the clock. This prevents gamesmanship in the coordination between ITC investigations and parallel patent litigation in district courts, particularly in pharmaceutical patent disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders pursuing parallel ITC and district court actions benefit from certainty that respondents cannot manipulate stay deadlines through refiling tactics, preserving the ability to litigate in both forums.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the 30-day deadline to seek a mandatory stay of district court proceedings cannot reset the clock by refiling, potentially forcing them to litigate on two fronts simultaneously.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform communication constellations with increased capacity are patent-eligible under § 101, and whether the patent holder's damages model was properly admitted.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain asserted claims of patents covering non-uniform constellations in digital communication systems while affirming eligibility for other claims, affirming the denial of JMOL on infringement and damages. The mixed ruling in this case involving ATSC 3.0 broadcast television standards has broad implications for standard-essential patent enforcement and the eligibility of applied mathematical optimization patents in telecommunications.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with claims tied to specific technical implementations of optimized communication systems (rather than abstract mathematical concepts) benefit from the court's affirmance of eligibility for certain claim formulations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies implementing industry standards face continued uncertainty about the eligibility of standard-essential patents, and manufacturers like LG face potential willful infringement liability for standards-compliant products.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative testimony is admissible at summary judgment despite the witness's lack of personal knowledge, and whether source code constitutes hearsay under the Federal Rules of Evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment invalidating engine controller reprogramming patents under the on-sale bar of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b), holding that Rule 30(b)(6) testimony is admissible regardless of the representative's personal knowledge and that computer source code commands are not hearsay. The evidentiary rulings have broad implications for patent invalidity defenses relying on corporate testimony about historical product sales and technical prior art evidence.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies defending against patent infringement can rely on Rule 30(b)(6) corporate testimony about historical sales and technical capabilities to establish prior art, even when the designee joined the company after the relevant events.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased vulnerability to on-sale bar challenges when historical corporate knowledge about prior art products can be introduced through 30(b)(6) witnesses without requiring personal knowledge.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the plaintiff presented legally sufficient evidence to establish that the asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether ideas that are generally known can constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims related to cosmetic penile implant technology, finding insufficient evidence that the four asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law because the underlying information was generally known. The court also reversed on patent inventorship, holding that contributions of generally known ideas cannot constitute inventive contributions. This decision sets an important standard for what qualifies as protectable trade secret information versus general industry knowledge.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret cases benefit from heightened scrutiny of whether asserted secrets are truly protectable rather than generally known information in the relevant industry.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret holders face greater risk of losing protection when their claimed secrets overlap with generally known industry information, even after obtaining favorable jury verdicts.

impacts.caseName: National Veterans Legal Services Program v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users, including the award of attorneys' fees, costs, and incentive awards to class representatives.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed approval of a $125 million nationwide class action settlement resolving claims that the federal judiciary exceeded its statutory authority by using PACER fees to fund projects unrelated to PACER operations. The court upheld the settlement terms, attorneys' fees, and incentive awards to nonprofit class representatives, rejecting an objector's challenges. This is one of the largest class settlements against the federal government and directly impacts hundreds of thousands of PACER users, including law firms, legal organizations, and businesses that regularly access federal court records.
impacts.positiveImplications: PACER users, including law firms and businesses, will receive full or substantial reimbursement of excessive PACER fees paid during the eight-year class period, and the settlement may constrain future PACER fee increases.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in excluding a patent holder's damages expert report for using a top-down methodology and in granting summary judgment based on absence of a damages remedy.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report in a patent infringement case against Microsoft's Azure platform, holding that the district court improperly excluded the expert's top-down damages methodology. The court also vacated summary judgment that had been entered based on the absence of a remedy after the expert exclusion. This decision clarifies the permissibility of top-down damages methodologies in patent cases and limits courts' ability to dispose of meritorious infringement claims by excluding damages evidence.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from broader acceptance of top-down damages methodologies, preserving their ability to present reasonable royalty calculations in complex technology patent cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies defending patent infringement actions face reduced ability to defeat claims through Daubert challenges to damages experts using top-down analytical frameworks.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTO Director's instructions to the Board governing discretionary denials of inter partes review institution are 'general statements of policy' exempt from APA notice-and-comment rulemaking requirements.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the PTO Director's instructions guiding Board decisions on whether to exercise discretion to deny IPR institution are general statements of policy exempt from APA notice-and-comment rulemaking under 5 U.S.C. § 553(b). The court emphasized that Congress provided no legal right to IPR institution, the Director retains ultimate authority over institution decisions, and the instructions do not bind the Director. This decision preserves the PTO's flexibility in managing its IPR docket without formal rulemaking constraints.
impacts.positiveImplications: The PTO retains flexibility to adjust IPR institution policies without burdensome rulemaking procedures, allowing responsive patent quality management.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that rely on IPR as a cost-effective alternative to district court litigation face continued uncertainty from discretionary denials that cannot be challenged as procedurally defective.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board erred in its obviousness determination of sensor-based logistics patent claims, including the construction of a 'predetermined time delay' limitation in restricting access to shipment sensor information.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness determination regarding FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded, finding errors in how the Board analyzed the prior art. The case also raised issues about whether a third party (Qualcomm) filed IPR petitions as a proxy for the time-barred defendant (Roambee), implicating the IPR time-bar provisions of 35 U.S.C. § 315(b). This decision has implications for supply chain technology patents and the use of proxy IPR petitioners to circumvent statutory filing deadlines.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in logistics and supply chain technology benefit from closer scrutiny of proxy IPR petitions that may be filed to circumvent time-bar provisions, protecting their patents from strategic challenges.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies seeking to challenge patents through IPR face constraints when relying on third-party petitioners, particularly when the timing and relationship suggest coordination with time-barred parties.
